segments.text: This topic explains the mercantilist logic underlying Britain’s pre-1783 Atlantic empire, and why the American crisis (Topics 2 and 4) exposed that system’s structural limits — directly setting up Britain’s later imperial reorientation.

blocks.text: Mercantilism, Navigation Acts and Plantation Economies

segments.text: European governments in this era generally believed national power depended on controlling trade, shipping and bullion flows; colonies were expected to supply raw materials, purchase metropolitan manufactured goods, and strengthen imperial commerce accordingly.

blocks.text: Colonial Institutions and the Path to Crisis

segments.text: Many mainland American colonies developed elected assemblies and local traditions of self-taxation and self-government, institutions that encouraged colonists to regard internal taxation as something requiring their own consent — directly explaining the constitutional shock produced by post-1763 British revenue measures (Topic 2). Britain and France competed extensively across North America, the Caribbean, and elsewhere; victory in the Seven Years’ War expanded British territory but also generated the debt and administrative burden that triggered the taxation disputes leading to American independence.

blocks.text: After America: A New Imperial Direction

segments.text: Following American independence, Britain increasingly redirected imperial expansion toward Asia, the Pacific, and Africa, producing an empire considerably more geographically diverse and administratively varied than the earlier, more narrowly Atlantic mercantilist system — a transition that connects directly into the imperial themes of Topics 9 and 13.

items.text: The economic doctrine that national power depends on controlling trade, shipping and bullion, with colonies serving the metropolitan economy.
Legislation regulating colonial shipping and trade in favour of English/British commercial interests.
Define mercantilism clearly; use the American colonies as the main case but connect them explicitly to the Caribbean and the Atlantic slave economy.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “How did the mercantilist old colonial system’s own internal tensions contribute to the American crisis?”
Do not define mercantilism as simply “selling more than buying”; it also involved regulation, shipping, monopoly and imperial power.
Do not discuss the old colonial system without slavery and plantation economies — they were central, not peripheral.
Do not imply all colonies were governed through one identical constitutional model.
Mercantilist policy sought to channel colonial trade for the benefit of the imperial economy.
Navigation legislation regulated shipping and colonial commerce in favour of English/British interests.
Plantation colonies in the Caribbean relied heavily on enslaved African labour and were economically central to the empire.
After 1763, new taxes and tighter imperial controls intensified conflict in mainland North America.
After American independence, Britain’s empire continued and expanded in other parts of the world.
The old colonial system was a regulated, mercantilist Atlantic commercial system built substantially on enslaved labour — both facts must appear together in any strong answer.

The same colonial assemblies that made the mercantilist system administratively workable also produced the self-government expectations that made post-1763 taxation disputes an existential constitutional crisis.
Loss of America redirected, rather than ended, British imperial ambition — directly connecting to the empire discussed in Topics 9 and 13.
